lead: An ideal transformer is a lossless two-coil block that changes AC voltage, current and impedance by the turns ratio alone. It assumes no winding resistance, no core loss, infinite core permeability and perfect coupling. A linear transformer is the practical coupled-coil model: finite self-inductances L₁ and L₂ and mutual inductance M. The ideal case is its limit. Transformers appear in phone chargers, adapters, isolation units and distribution, where they step voltage down and match impedance.
prereq: You need: M, k and the dot convention, and phasor mesh analysis.

sections.h3: Ideal transformer: voltage, current and impedance

blocks.text: Let N₁ and N₂ be the turns on the primary and secondary coils. Define the turns ratio n = N₂/N₁. With the dots at the same polarity, the secondary voltage is V₂ = nV₁. If the secondary current I₂ leaves the dotted terminal and the primary current I₁ enters its dot, ampere-turn balance N₁I₁ = N₂I₂ gives I₂/I₁ = N₁/N₂ = 1/n. Power in equals power out: V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ for resistive loading.
n = N₂/N₁; V₂/V₁ = n; I₂/I₁ = 1/n; Zin = (N₁/N₂)² ZL

Here n is the turns ratio (dimensionless); N₁ and N₂ are primary and secondary turns; V₁ and V₂ are rms voltages; I₁ and I₂ are rms currents with I₂ leaving the dotted secondary terminal; Z<sub>in</sub> is the impedance seen at the primary; Z<sub>L</sub> is the load impedance on the secondary, in ohms.

items: No winding resistance: copper loss is zero.
No core loss: hysteresis and eddy-current loss are zero.
Infinite core permeability: finite flux needs zero magnetizing current.
Perfect coupling k = 1: no leakage flux links only one coil.

blocks.text: The ideal transformer is a limiting case, not a component you can buy. It fixes voltage, current and impedance ratios but draws no magnetizing current and stores no energy. Seen from the primary, a load Z<sub>L</sub> looks like Z<sub>L</sub>/n²; this is the referred (reflected) load used for impedance matching.

A linear transformer keeps finite L₁, L₂ and M = k√(L₁L₂), where k is the coefficient of coupling; ω is the source's angular frequency in rad/s. Take both dots at the top and let mesh current I₂ enter the dotted secondary terminal. This is the opposite of the load current used for the ideal ratios above, so the load current is −I₂. Winding resistances are omitted here; add R₁ and R₂ in series with L₁ and L₂ when they matter.

V₁ = jωL₁I₁ + jωM I₂
0 = jωM I₁ + (jωL₂ + ZL)I₂
Zin = V₁/I₁ = jωL₁ + (ωM)²/(jωL₂ + ZL)

Here v₁ is the primary source voltage; I₁ is the primary mesh current; I₂ is the secondary mesh current entering the dotted terminal; L₁ and L₂ are self-inductances in henries; M is mutual inductance in henries; ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s; Z<sub>L</sub> is the load impedance in ohms; Z<sub>in</sub> is the input impedance in ohms.

Eliminate I₂: I₂ = −jωM I₁/(jωL₂ + Z<sub>L</sub>). Substitution gives the input impedance above. The second term, (ωM)²/(jωL₂ + Z<sub>L</sub>), is the reflected impedance: the secondary as the primary sees it. If either dot is reversed, the sign of every jωM term flips; Z<sub>in</sub> does not change because M appears squared, but I₂ and V₂ change phase by 180°.

Magnetizing current is the primary current that sets the core flux. A finite L₁ draws this current even with no load. Because L grows as N², the ideal transformer is the limit L₁ → ∞ with k = 1 and L₂/L₁ = n² held fixed; then the magnetizing current goes to zero and the turns-ratio laws hold exactly.

sections.h3: Use, limits and a step-change note

blocks.text: A charger transformer steps 230 V AC down to a low AC voltage, then rectifies it. A distribution transformer steps voltage down for homes and isolates the load from the feeder. Impedance scaling is useful: a 10 Ω load on the secondary can look like 250 Ω at the primary when N₁/N₂ = 5.

A real transformer has copper loss, core loss, leakage flux and finite magnetizing inductance. The linear model keeps finite L₁, L₂ and M; the ideal model is its limit. Reluctance and flux in the core are worked out in magnetic circuits.

With a sudden voltage step, the ideal model lets currents jump instantly in the ratio set by the turns, because ampere-turn balance must hold at every instant. A real coil has finite L, so its current rises with a time constant of order L/R; that is a first-order transient.

spec.aria: A transformer core with a 500-turn primary on a 230 volt source and a 100-turn secondary feeding a 10 ohm load, with dots, currents 0.92 and 4.6 amps, secondary voltage 46 volts and the referred impedance 250 ohms.

examples.question: An ideal transformer has N₁ = 500 turns, N₂ = 100 turns, primary voltage 230 V rms and a 10 Ω load on the secondary. Find V₂, I₂, I₁ and Z<sub>in</sub>.
steps: Secondary voltage V₂ = nV₁ = 0.2 × 230 V = 46 V rms.
Secondary current I₂ = V₂/Z<sub>L</sub> = 46 V / 10 Ω = 4.6 A rms.
Primary current I₁ = nI₂ = 0.2 × 4.6 A = 0.92 A rms.
Input impedance Z<sub>in</sub> = (N₁/N₂)²Z<sub>L</sub> = (500/100)² × 10 Ω = 25 × 10 Ω = 250 Ω.
Power check: V₁I₁ = 230 × 0.92 = 211.6 W and V₂I₂ = 46 × 4.6 = 211.6 W.
examples.answer: V₂ = 46 V rms, I₂ = 4.6 A rms, I₁ = 0.92 A rms and Z<sub>in</sub> = 250 Ω.

examples.question: A linear transformer has L₁ = 0.2 H, L₂ = 0.8 H and M = 0.3 H. It is driven by 10∠0° V at ω = 100 rad/s and feeds a 10 Ω load. Find k, Z<sub>in</sub>, I₁, |I₂| and the load power.
steps: Reactances: ωL₁ = 20 Ω, ωL₂ = 80 Ω, ωM = 30 Ω, so (ωM)² = 900 Ω².
Load power: 0.412² × 10 = 1.70 W. Check: |I₁|² × Re(Z<sub>in</sub>) = 1.107² × 1.385 = 1.70 W, so all the input power reaches the load.

traps: Turns ratio direction: n = N₂/N₁ for voltage, but the current ratio is 1/n. With the secondary current leaving the dot, I₂/I₁ = N₁/N₂. Students often invert both.

Impedance reflects by the square of the turns ratio, and the direction matters. Seen from the primary, Z<sub>in</sub> = (N₁/N₂)²Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>L</sub>/n²; seen from the secondary, a primary impedance looks n² times larger. Write the direction before squaring.
The ideal transformer is the limit of a linear transformer as L₁, L₂ and M go to infinity with k = 1. Do not use the ideal ratio on a finite-L linear transformer without checking magnetizing current.
Dot reversal changes the sign of jωM in the mesh equations and the phase of V₂ by 180°. Magnitudes stay the same, so a dot question is usually about sign and phase.
Keep units: n is dimensionless, Z<sub>in</sub> and Z<sub>L</sub> are in ohms, V is in volts rms, I is in amperes rms and ω is in rad/s.

quiz.q: Define turns ratio n and state the ideal voltage ratio with dots at the same polarity.
Why does an ideal transformer draw zero magnetizing current?
quiz.a: Infinite core permeability makes finite flux need zero magnetizing MMF; the ideal model is the limit L₁ → ∞ with k = 1.

quiz.q: An ideal transformer has N₁ = 800, N₂ = 200, V₁ = 120 V rms and Z<sub>L</sub> = 8 Ω. Find V₂, I₂, I₁ and Z<sub>in</sub>.
Explain from power balance why an ideal transformer scales impedance by n² and not by n.
quiz.a: Voltage scales by n and current scales by 1/n, so V/I scales by n². Power V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ stays unchanged.

quiz.q: A linear transformer has its dot on the secondary reversed. How do the mesh equations and the phase of V₂ change?
quiz.a: The sign of each jωM term flips. V₂ changes phase by 180°, while the magnitude ratios stay the same.

quiz.q: The linear transformer of the second worked example (L₁ = 0.2 H, L₂ = 0.8 H, M = 0.3 H, ω = 100 rad/s) has its secondary short-circuited. Find Z<sub>in</sub>.
quiz.a: Z<sub>L</sub> = 0, so Z<sub>in</sub> = jωL₁ + (ωM)²/(jωL₂) = j20 + 900/(j80) = j20 − j11.25 = j8.75 Ω. This equals jω(L₁ − M²/L₂) = j100 × 0.0875: the short leaves only the uncoupled part of L₁.

quiz.q: What is magnetizing current in a linear transformer?
quiz.a: It is the primary current that sets the core flux. Finite L₁ draws it even at no load; it tends to zero as L₁ → ∞.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phone chargers use planar transformers with ferrite cores and finite magnetizing inductance; designing them needs the linear model plus core loss. RF circuits use transmission-line transformers for impedance matching. Power engineers simulate transformers with finite-element tools and check inrush and saturation. Search next for "transformer magnetizing inductance", "dot convention" and "impedance matching transformer".
